# Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** Hardware expansion decision for the inference fleet

## The situation

Our inference cluster has been running hot for about six weeks. Peak-hour GPU utilisation sits in the high eighties, queue times during business hours have crept from negligible to noticeable, and we've had two incidents where batch jobs starved the interactive serving path. The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the two options are not symmetric and the framing matters more than the spreadsheet.

## What buying gets us — and what it costs

Purchasing more hardware is the blunt instrument, and sometimes blunt is right. Capital expenditure for a meaningful expansion would be substantial, and beyond the sticker price there's the operational tail: rack space, power, cooling, and the engineering time to integrate and monitor new nodes. None of that is exotic, but it all compounds. The real argument for buying is latency and headroom. If our traffic keeps growing the way it has, additional capacity restores comfortable margins immediately, and it insulates us from the kind of contention-driven incidents we saw last month. There's also a reliability argument: more nodes means more graceful degradation when something fails, and right now a single node going down pushes us uncomfortably close to the edge.

But buying has a hidden cost that's easy to undervalue: opportunity cost. Every dollar spent on capacity we may not need in six months is a dollar not spent on the model-quality work and tooling improvements that arguably drive more user value per unit of spend. Hardware also depreciates and locks us into a particular architecture at a moment when the vendor landscape is shifting quickly.

## What better utilisation gets us — and where it falls short

The case for improving utilisation rests on the observation that our average utilisation is meaningfully lower than our peak. That gap is where the opportunity lives. Right now, batch inference and interactive serving compete for the same resources with only crude priority controls. Better scheduling, dynamic batching tuned to our actual latency targets, and smarter model placement could plausibly recover twenty to thirty percent of effective capacity without buying anything. That's real money, and the work itself — better observability, better queueing discipline — pays dividends regardless of what we decide later.

The risk is that utilisation work is engineering work, and engineering work takes time we may not have. If peak demand keeps climbing while we're mid-refactor, we could spend a quarter optimising and still end up capacity-constrained, having traded user-visible latency for internal elegance. There's also a ceiling: no amount of scheduling cleverness creates capacity that doesn't exist. If our true demand exceeds our true supply, utilisation improvements just move the cliff edge rather than removing it.

## Reversibility, and why it tips the balance

The asymmetry that matters most is reversibility. Buying hardware is a one-way door in practice — once capital is committed and machines are racked, unwinding that decision is slow and lossy. Improving utilisation is a two-way door: the scheduling and batching work is valuable even if we later buy hardware, and nothing about it forecloses expansion. When one option preserves optionality and the other consumes it, the option-preserving path deserves the benefit of the doubt, especially under uncertainty about whether our demand curve is a trend or a spike.

## Recommendation

My recommendation is to invest the next six to eight weeks in the utilisation work — dynamic batching, scheduling improvements, and proper per-tenant capacity accounting — while simultaneously doing the procurement legwork so that a purchase order is ready to execute if the numbers justify it. Set a concrete trigger now: if, after the optimisation work lands, peak utilisation still exceeds roughly eighty-five percent or interactive latency breaches our SLO more than twice in a month, we execute the purchase without relitigating. This sequencing costs us a little time risk, but it converts a permanent capital decision into a conditional one.

## Uncertainty

I want to be honest about what I don't know. Our demand forecast is based on six weeks of data, which is thin. The utilisation gains I've cited are estimates from preliminary profiling, not measured results, and they could be half of what I've suggested. And the engineering effort for the scheduling work may be larger than scoped if our current placement logic is more tangled than it appears. If any of those uncertainties resolve badly, the case for buying strengthens considerably — which is exactly why the trigger-based approach above is the right shape for this decision.

Happy to walk through the numbers with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** Inference capacity strategy for the next two quarters

**Status: For discussion ahead of Thursday's decision meeting**

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Peak-hour GPU utilisation sits in the high eighties, queue times during the morning and late-afternoon bursts have crept from tens of milliseconds into the seconds range, and two of our internal customers have started asking, politely but pointedly, whether we can guarantee latency. The obvious question on the table is whether we should buy more hardware. My argument in this memo is that we should not — not yet — and that the next six weeks should go into raising utilisation on the fleet we already own, with a purchase decision deferred until we have evidence we actually need it.

Start with the economics. The capital cost of another node is not just the sticker price. It's the rack space, the power draw, the cooling headroom we'd consume, and — less visibly — the engineering time to integrate, monitor, and maintain it. Against that, our current fleet is demonstrably underused in aggregate even while it's overused at peak. Our own telemetry shows utilisation dropping below twenty percent overnight and on weekends, and even during business hours there are long stretches where individual nodes idle because workloads are pinned to them rather than scheduled dynamically. Buying more hardware now would mean paying to add capacity at the same moment we're leaving a third or more of our existing capacity unused. That's the opportunity cost in its purest form: every dollar spent on new iron is a dollar not spent on the scheduling work, the batching improvements, and the observability gaps that got us into this position.

The counterargument, and it's a fair one, is latency. Scheduling improvements and better batching reduce average latency, but they don't reliably shave the tail. If our product commitments require p99 latency under a hard threshold, there's a limit to how far clever software can carry us on fixed hardware. I don't think we're at that limit yet — our tail latency is currently driven mostly by cold starts and unbatched single-request traffic, both of which are tractable — but I want to be honest that this is the scenario where my recommendation ages badly. If the utilisation work stalls and the tail stays ugly, buying hardware becomes the right call quickly, and we should not let sunk effort into optimisation delay that decision out of stubbornness.

Reliability cuts both ways, and it's worth spelling out. More nodes means more redundancy: a single node failure today degrades service noticeably, whereas a larger fleet would absorb it. But more nodes also means more failure surface, more drivers to keep in sync, and more of our small team's attention divided. Improving utilisation, by contrast, pushes us toward a more homogeneous, dynamically scheduled fleet — which, done well, actually improves reliability because any node can pick up any request. The risk is the transition itself: rescheduling workloads is exactly the kind of change that causes incidents if rushed. I'd propose we do it behind feature flags, node by node, with a rollback path at every step.

That points to the strongest reason for my recommendation, which is reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale. The money is spent, the depreciation clock starts, and if our workload mix shifts — say, a model change halves our compute per request — we're carrying capacity we can't return. Utilisation work is the opposite: nearly every intervention is reversible, cheap to undo, and generates information we'd want even if we eventually buy hardware anyway. Understanding our true demand curve, our batching efficiency, and our real peak-to-trough ratio is prerequisite knowledge for a purchase done right. Buying first and learning later gets that backwards.

So the recommendation: commit the next six weeks to dynamic scheduling, request batching, and off-peak job migration, with explicit latency SLOs measured throughout. Set a concrete trigger now — for example, if p99 latency breaches our target for more than a defined number of hours in a week despite these changes — so that the follow-on purchase decision is mechanical rather than debated from scratch. Acknowledge the uncertainty: our traffic may simply be growing fast enough that optimisation buys us one quarter, not two. But one quarter of better information, at near-zero cost and full reversibility, is worth more to a team our size than an early purchase we might regret.

Comments welcome before Thursday.

# Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** Inference capacity decision for the next two quarters

## The situation

Our inference fleet is running hot. Peak-hour GPU utilisation on the primary cluster has been sitting around 85–90% for the past six weeks, queue times during business hours have crept from negligible to 200–400 milliseconds, and we've had two brief incidents where batch jobs backed up interactive traffic enough to breach our internal latency SLO. The obvious question on the table is whether we buy more hardware. The less obvious question — and the one I think we should answer first — is whether we're actually using what we own.

## The case for buying

Buying is simple and fast. A modest expansion — two to four additional nodes — would cost roughly $120–180K in capital, plus power, cooling, and rack space we've already provisioned for. Lead times are currently four to six weeks, which is annoying but tolerable. The upside is real: headroom is headroom, and it removes the latency tail risk immediately. It also gives us a buffer for the two new product launches planned for next quarter, whose traffic forecasts are, as always, educated guesses.

But buying has a cost beyond the invoice. Capital spent on hardware is capital not spent on engineering time, and right now our utilisation problem is partly an engineering problem. We're running three model variants that could plausibly be consolidated. Our batching window is conservative. We have no meaningful autoscaling of batch workloads away from peak hours. Every one of those is a fixable inefficiency, and every GPU we buy at 85% utilisation is a GPU we buy at a discount to its real price.

## The case for improving utilisation

The utilisation work is cheaper in cash terms — call it six to eight weeks of one senior engineer's time, plus some review from the rest of us — but it is slower and, critically, it is not guaranteed to work. Consolidating model variants carries regression risk. Aggressive batching improves throughput but adds latency variance, which is exactly what we're trying to reduce. If the utilisation project stalls or delivers half its projected gains, we'll have spent six weeks and still need to buy hardware, now with less calendar runway before the product launches.

There's also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More headroom from new hardware is a genuine reliability improvement — it absorbs traffic spikes and lets us fail over during node maintenance. But so does better scheduling: right now, a single misbehaving batch job can degrade interactive traffic, and that's a fragility no amount of hardware fully fixes.

## Reversibility matters more than it looks

Here's the asymmetry I keep coming back to. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible commitment. GPUs depreciate, our rack space is finite, and reselling at anything close to book value is optimistic. Utilisation work, by contrast, is highly reversible — if a batching change hurts latency, we roll it back in an afternoon. When one option is reversible and the other isn't, and both plausibly address the problem, the reversible option deserves the first attempt. That's not a hard rule, but it's a good default when the downside of trying is measured in weeks rather than dollars.

## Recommendation

Do the utilisation work first, but pre-authorise the hardware purchase so we're not starting from zero if it falls short. Concretely: spend the next six weeks on model consolidation and dynamic batching, with a target of bringing peak utilisation below 70% and p99 latency back under our SLO. In parallel, get procurement quotes now and secure budget approval, so that if we miss the target — or if launch traffic forecasts come in high — we can place the order immediately rather than in week ten of a crisis. If utilisation work delivers even 60% of projected gains, we likely defer the purchase a full quarter and buy with better information about next year's real demand.

## Uncertainty, honestly stated

The biggest unknown is our own traffic forecast. If the launches double interactive load, no realistic utilisation gain covers it, and buying becomes the right call regardless of efficiency. The second unknown is engineering bandwidth — the utilisation project assumes we can actually spare the senior time, and if we can't, the whole plan is fiction. I'd rather discover that now than in week four.

Let's discuss at Thursday's planning session. My ask is a decision on the pre-authorisation, not the purchase itself.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** This week

---

We've been circling the same question for about six weeks now: do we spend money on more local AI hardware, or do we invest the same effort in squeezing more out of the machines we already own? I want to lay out how I see the trade-offs, make a recommendation, and be honest about where I might be wrong.

First, the situation as it stands. Our current fleet runs hot during working hours and nearly idle overnight and on weekends. Peak utilisation on the training nodes sits around 85–90%, but the weekly average is closer to 40%. Inference capacity is tighter — we've had two incidents this quarter where batch jobs were queued behind interactive workloads, and one where a customer-facing feature degraded because a fine-tuning run overran its window. So the pain is real, but it's a peak problem, not a capacity problem. That distinction matters for everything below.

The case for buying is straightforward: hardware is cheap relative to engineering time, and it's the fastest way to make the pain disappear. A new node arrives, we rack it, the queues clear, and nobody has to think about scheduling again. Latency for interactive work improves immediately and predictably. There's also a reliability argument — right now, a single node failure during a critical run means either delay or emergency triage, because we have no headroom to absorb it. Redundancy is a luxury we currently don't have, and buying capacity is the simplest way to buy it.

But the case for better utilisation is stronger than it first appears, for three reasons.

The first is cost, and specifically the shape of the cost. Buying hardware is a capital decision with a long tail: the purchase price is only the beginning. Power, cooling, rack space, and — more importantly in our case — the ongoing operational burden of maintaining more machines fall on a team of five. Every additional node is something we must patch, monitor, and eventually decommission. Improving utilisation, by contrast, costs mostly engineering time we'd spend anyway, and the payoff compounds: a scheduler improvement that lifts average utilisation from 40% to 60% is effectively two free nodes, without two nodes' worth of maintenance.

The second is opportunity cost. The engineering effort to build proper job queueing, checkpointing, and off-peak scheduling is real — call it three to four weeks of one or two engineers. But that work also produces capabilities we'll want regardless: better checkpointing makes us more resilient to hardware failure even on the fleet we have, and a proper queue makes our latency behaviour legible to the rest of the company. Buying hardware, by contrast, consumes budget that could go to data licensing or a contractor, and it teaches us nothing.

The third is reversibility, and this is where I think the decision actually turns. Hardware purchases are nearly irreversible at our scale. If we buy a node and demand shifts — a model gets smaller, a workload moves to a vendor, priorities change — we're carrying depreciating silicon we can't easily sell. Utilisation work is the opposite: it's a set of software decisions we can adjust, extend, or abandon as circumstances change. In an environment where our AI roadmap is still genuinely uncertain, I'd rather hold the option than lock in the capacity.

So my recommendation: do not buy hardware now. Instead, spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation — a shared job queue with priorities, mandatory checkpointing for long runs, and moving batch workloads into the overnight window. Set a concrete trigger for revisiting the purchase: if interactive jobs queue for more than fifteen minutes at peak for two consecutive weeks, or if we lose a node and can't absorb its workload, we buy, and we buy without further debate. That trigger converts a fuzzy judgement call into a measurable condition, which is the best I can offer given how noisy our demand signal is.

Where I could be wrong: if our inference traffic is about to grow sharply — say, a feature launch next quarter — the utilisation work won't scale fast enough, and the six weeks we spend optimising will look like time we should have spent procuring. I've asked the product side for their forecast, and I'd encourage anyone with visibility there to push back on this memo if the growth story is credible. I'd also rather be a month late buying hardware than a month early, but reasonable people can weight that differently.

Let's discuss at Thursday's sync, with a decision to follow by end of week.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** This week

---

We've been circling the same question for about six weeks now: do we spend money on more local AI hardware, or do we invest the same effort in squeezing more out of the machines we already own? I want to lay out how I see the trade-offs, make a recommendation, and be honest about where my confidence is thin.

First, the situation as it stands. Our four inference nodes run at roughly 40–55% utilisation during business hours, with nightly training jobs pushing two of them to saturation. Peak demand — the Monday morning batch and the end-of-quarter evaluation runs — occasionally queues for hours. Meanwhile, the hardware itself is fine. Nothing is failing, nothing is end-of-life, and our maintenance burden has actually been lower than we budgeted for.

The case for buying more is straightforward: it removes the ceiling. If the team's roadmap — the real-time assistant work, the growing fine-tuning backlog — lands the way we hope, demand will eventually exceed what four nodes can deliver no matter how clever our scheduling gets. Buying now also means we're not making that purchase in a panic later, at whatever prices prevail then. And there's a reliability argument: a fifth node gives us genuine redundancy. Right now, losing a node during a training window means dropping a job or delaying a release. That's a real operational risk, not a hypothetical one.

But the case for improving utilisation is stronger than it first appears, and I want to make sure we don't skip past it. The gap between our average utilisation and our peak is not a hardware problem; it's a scheduling and hygiene problem. Jobs sit queued because nobody has written a proper priority system. Two of our nodes idle every weekend because the batch scheduler doesn't pack work across them. Some of the fine-tuning backlog is stale — experiments people have quietly abandoned but never cancelled. I'd estimate, conservatively, that better queueing, time-slicing for inference, and cleaning up zombie jobs gets us to 70–75% effective utilisation without buying anything. That's the equivalent of adding nearly two nodes for the cost of a few engineering weeks.

Then there's opportunity cost, which I think is the crux. The money for new hardware is real but finite, and every dollar spent on silicon is a dollar not spent on the observability tooling and the model-evaluation pipeline we keep saying we need. More importantly, the engineering time to integrate and operate new hardware is time not spent on the product work that justifies the hardware's existence in the first place. Buying capacity to run jobs we haven't validated yet is a way of deferring decisions rather than making them.

Reversibility matters too, and it cuts both ways. Hardware is a lumpy, semi-irreversible commitment — depreciation is slow, resale is painful, and if our workload shifts (say, toward hosted inference for latency-sensitive paths), we're stuck holding capacity we can't easily repurpose. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely reversible: if a scheduling change turns out to hurt latency, we roll it back in an afternoon. That asymmetry argues for exhausting the software options first.

On latency, I want to be careful not to overstate the local-versus-hosted question. Our local inference latency is good and improving utilisation won't degrade it if we're sensible about isolation. The latency risk comes from over-packing — running inference and training on the same node without proper partitioning. That's a solvable engineering problem, not a reason to buy hardware.

So, my recommendation: spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation — a real scheduler with priorities, batch packing across all four nodes, and a purge of stale jobs — and set a concrete trigger for purchase. If, after that, we still see queueing on peak days, or if the real-time assistant work slips because of contention, we buy one node, not two, and revisit. I'd put my confidence at maybe 70% that this defers the purchase indefinitely rather than merely delaying it, which is exactly the outcome we want: we buy when demand is proven, not when anxiety is high.

The honest uncertainty here is about our own roadmap. If the team doubles in the next quarter, all of this arithmetic changes. Let's revisit in eight weeks with real numbers.

Comments welcome before Friday's planning session.
